q: The outermost shell electrons (____) of those atoms are the basis for understanding the joining of atoms.
e: The outermost shell electrons (valence electrons) of those atoms are the basis for understanding the joining of atoms. Those outer electrons are the ones that join atoms together.

q: In order to explain the electronic structures of atoms, the principles of filling electrons in the atomic orbitals, such as the ____, Pauli's exclusion principle, and Hund's rule are fundamental to understand.
e: In order to explain the electronic structures of atoms, the principles of filling electrons in the atomic orbitals, such as the Aufbau principle, Pauli's exclusion principle, and Hund's rule are fundamental to understand. Aufbau means you fill lower-energy orbitals first, and only then climb into higher-energy ones.

q: In atoms, there are K, L, M, N,... main shells and each main shell can be divided into s, p, d, and f ____.
e: In atoms, there are K, L, M, N,... main shells and each main shell can be divided into s, p, d, and f subshells. Each main shell splits into s, p, d, and f subshells.

q: Each subshell can be filled with 2, 6, 10, and ____ electrons, respectively.
e: Each subshell can be filled with 2, 6, 10, and 14 electrons, respectively. The f subshell holds fourteen electrons after s, p, and d take 2, 6, and 10.

q: In addition, s subshell has only one ____-shaped orbital.
e: In addition, s subshell has only one spherical-shaped orbital. An s orbital is spherical.

q: There are three ____-shaped p orbitals (px, py, pz) and the five d orbitals have double dumbbell-shapes.
e: There are three dumbbell-shaped p orbitals (px, py, pz) and the five d orbitals have double dumbbell-shapes. P orbitals are dumbbells along x, y, and z.

q: According to the Aufbau principle (Aufbau means building up in German), electrons are filled in the ____ energy atomic orbitals before filling higher energy ones.
e: According to the Aufbau principle (Aufbau means building up in German), electrons are filled in the lower energy atomic orbitals before filling higher energy ones. Aufbau fills lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy ones.

q: Each electron spins on an ____, like a globe.
e: Each electron spins on an axis, like a globe. Axis is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: Pauli's exclusion principle states that no more than two electrons can occupy the same orbital, and two electrons in the same orbital must have ____ spins.
e: Pauli's exclusion principle states that no more than two electrons can occupy the same orbital, and two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins. Two electrons in one orbital must spin opposite ways.

q: Hund's rule states that every orbital in a subshell is ____ occupied with one electron before any one orbital is doubly occupied with opposite spins, and all electrons in singly occupied orbitals have the same spin.
e: Hund's rule states that every orbital in a subshell is singly occupied with one electron before any one orbital is doubly occupied with opposite spins, and all electrons in singly occupied orbitals have the same spin. Hund occupies each orbital once before pairing.

q: The electrons in the ____ shells (outermost shells) of an atom are known as the valence electrons.
e: The electrons in the valence shells (outermost shells) of an atom are known as the valence electrons. Valence means the outermost shell that bonds.

q: For an atom, the number of valence electrons is equal to its ____ number in the Periodic Table.
e: For an atom, the number of valence electrons is equal to its group number in the Periodic Table. For a main-group atom, valence electrons equal the group number.

q: Only ____ electrons can take part in chemical bonding.
e: Only valence electrons can take part in chemical bonding. Valence means the outermost shell that bonds.

q: Whenever a chemical bond forms, atoms lose, gain, or share electrons in order to achieve the stable electronic structures of ____, i.e., eight electrons in the valence shell, which is known as the octet rule.
e: Whenever a chemical bond forms, atoms lose, gain, or share electrons in order to achieve the stable electronic structures of noble gases,, eight electrons in the valence shell, which is known as the octet rule. Noble-gas configurations are the stable targets of bonding.

q: To explain the chemical bonding and structures of atoms, molecules, and ions, the symbols introduced by ____ are used.
e: To explain the chemical bonding and structures of atoms, molecules, and ions, the symbols introduced by Gilbert Lewis are used. A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair and a Lewis base donates one.

q: Since ____ (EN) is a measure of the ability of an atom to attract the shared electrons to itself, the greater an element's electronegativity, the stronger its attractive power to electrons will be.
e: Since electronegativity (EN) is a measure of the ability of an atom to attract the shared electrons to itself, the greater an element's electronegativity, the stronger its attractive power to electrons will be. Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls shared bonding electrons toward itself.

q: In general, electron affinity (EA) is the amount of energy ____ when an electron is added to a gaseous atom, and ionisation energy (IE) is the amount of energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom.
e: In general, electron affinity (EA) is the amount of energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom, and ionisation energy (IE) is the amount of energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom. Energy is released when a gaseous atom gains an electron.

q: Therefore, the elements having high electron affinity easily gain electrons, resulting in the formation of the ____, and the elements having low ionisation energy easily lose electrons, resulting in the formation of the cations.
e: Therefore, the elements having high electron affinity easily gain electrons, resulting in the formation of the anions, and the elements having low ionisation energy easily lose electrons, resulting in the formation of the cations. Gaining electrons makes negative ions.

q: Generally, the higher the first ____ of an element, the greater is its electronegativity.
e: Generally, the higher the first ionisation energy of an element, the greater is its electronegativity. Ionisation energy is the energy you must put in to pull an electron off a gaseous atom.

q: There are three main types of chemical bonding, such as ionic bonding, covalent bonding, and ____ bonding.
e: There are three main types of chemical bonding, such as ionic bonding, covalent bonding, and metallic bonding. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: These weak forces, called ____ forces, are hydrogen bonding and van der Waals forces such as ion-dipole interaction, dipole-dipole interaction, and London dispersion forces.
e: These weak forces, called intermolecular forces, are hydrogen bonding and van der Waals forces such as ion-dipole interaction, dipole-dipole interaction, and London dispersion forces. London dispersion forces are weak temporary-dipole attractions found in every substance.

q: In general, an ionic bond is ____ than a covalent bond.
e: In general, an ionic bond is stronger than a covalent bond. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: The hydrogen bond is the ____ intermolecular force followed by van der Waals forces.
e: The hydrogen bond is the strongest intermolecular force followed by van der Waals forces. Strongest: intermolecular forces tug neighbouring molecules or ions together; they are not the bonds inside a molecule.

q: Among van der Waals forces, London dispersion forces are the ____ intermolecular forces that can be found in all substances.
e: Among van der Waals forces, London dispersion forces are the weakest intermolecular forces that can be found in all substances. Weakest: london dispersion forces are weak temporary-dipole attractions found in every substance.

q: Ionic bonding depends on the difference in ____ between two atoms.
e: Ionic bonding depends on the difference in electronegativity between two atoms. Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls shared bonding electrons toward itself.

q: Mostly it takes place when the difference in electronegativity is greater than ____.
e: Mostly it takes place when the difference in electronegativity is greater than 1.8. An electronegativity gap bigger than about 1.8 usually means ionic bonding.

q: When an ionic bond forms, a metal loses electrons to form positively charged ions (cations), whereas the non-metal atom readily ____ electrons to form negatively charged ions (anions).
e: When an ionic bond forms, a metal loses electrons to form positively charged ions (cations), whereas the non-metal atom readily gains electrons to form negatively charged ions (anions). The non-metal gains electrons while the metal loses them.

q: The two or more oppositely charged ions are then attracted to each other by strong ____ force, which is known as an ionic bond.
e: The two or more oppositely charged ions are then attracted to each other by strong electrostatic force, which is known as an ionic bond. Opposite ionic charges pull together in an ionic bond.

q: The number of lost or gained electrons by an atom during ionic bonding is the same as the ____ of that element.
e: The number of lost or gained electrons by an atom during ionic bonding is the same as the valency of that element. An ionic bond is the strong electrostatic pull between a cation and an anion after electrons transfer.

q: As a result, both ions, $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$, have the electronic configurations of ____ Ne and Ar, respectively.
e: As a result, both ions, Na+ and Cl-, have the electronic configurations of noble gases Ne and Ar, respectively. Noble-gas configurations are the stable targets of bonding.

q: The $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$ ions can be present only in a ____ ratio in the sodium chloride compound, so the formula must be NaCl.
e: The Na+ and Cl- ions can be present only in a 1:1 ratio in the sodium chloride compound, so the formula must be NaCl. 1:1 is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: In ionic compounds, the cations and anions are held together by strong ____ attraction.
e: In ionic compounds, the cations and anions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction. Opposite ionic charges pull together in an ionic bond.

q: In general, the greater the ____ on the ions, the greater the electrostatic attraction and the stronger the ionic bond will be.
e: In general, the greater the charge on the ions, the greater the electrostatic attraction and the stronger the ionic bond will be. Charge: an ionic bond is the strong electrostatic pull between a cation and an anion after electrons transfer.

q: So, the melting points of the ionic compounds with the greater charge on the ions are ____.
e: So, the melting points of the ionic compounds with the greater charge on the ions are higher. Ionic bonding is electron transfer followed by the pull between opposite ions.

q: In solid ionic compounds, their ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move, and hence they cannot ____ electricity.
e: In solid ionic compounds, their ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move, and hence they cannot conduct electricity. Conduct: ionic bonding is electron transfer followed by the pull between opposite ions.

q: In the crystalline state of ionic compounds, the oppositely charged ions are held together in orderly ____-dimensional arrangements, forming giant structures.
e: In the crystalline state of ionic compounds, the oppositely charged ions are held together in orderly three-dimensional arrangements, forming giant structures. Ionic bonding is electron transfer followed by the pull between opposite ions.

q: The crystalline structure of an ionic solid is called a ____, created by repeating unit cells.
e: The crystalline structure of an ionic solid is called a crystal lattice, created by repeating unit cells. A crystal lattice is the repeating three-dimensional pattern of atoms, ions, or molecules in a solid.

q: The cubic unit cell can have three types: simple cubic (sc) unit cell, ____ cubic (fcc) unit cell, and body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell, as shown in the illustrations.
e: The cubic unit cell can have three types: simple cubic (sc) unit cell, face-centred cubic (fcc) unit cell, and body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell, as shown in the illustrations. A simple cubic cell has atoms only at the eight corners of the cube.

q: For example, sodium chloride (rock salt, NaCl), a white crystalline solid, does not contain one $Na^+$ ion and one $Cl^-$ ion, but a lot of these two ions are arranged in a ____.
e: For example, sodium chloride (rock salt, NaCl), a white crystalline solid, does not contain one Na+ ion and one Cl- ion, but a lot of these two ions are arranged in a crystal lattice. A crystal lattice is the repeating three-dimensional pattern of atoms, ions, or molecules in a solid.

q: So, each $Na^+$ ion has ____ neighbouring $Cl^-$ ions, and each $Cl^-$ ion has six neighbouring $Na^+$ ions.
e: So, each Na+ ion has six neighbouring Cl- ions, and each Cl- ion has six neighbouring Na+ ions. Six is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: The term ____ is used to express the number of ions surrounding the central ion in the lattice.
e: The term coordination number is used to express the number of ions surrounding the central ion in the lattice. Coordination number counts how many neighbours surround a central atom or ion in the lattice.

q: Since the coordination ratio of $Na^+$ ion to $Cl^-$ ion is 6:6, the simple ratio of ____ gives the formula unit of sodium chloride which is NaCl.
e: Since the coordination ratio of Na+ ion to Cl- ion is 6:6, the simple ratio of 1:1 gives the formula unit of sodium chloride which is NaCl. 1:1 is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: Covalent bonding can occur between similar or even ____ atoms.
e: Covalent bonding can occur between similar or even identical atoms. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: The concept of electron ____ rather than electron transfer explains bonding between similar or identical atoms.
e: The concept of electron sharing rather than electron transfer explains bonding between similar or identical atoms. Sharing is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: As a result, a covalent bond is formed by sharing one or more pairs of ____ electrons between atoms.
e: As a result, a covalent bond is formed by sharing one or more pairs of valence electrons between atoms. Valence means the outermost shell that bonds.

q: Thus, the covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between the ____ of the atoms and the shared electrons.
e: Thus, the covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of the atoms and the shared electrons. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: Covalent bonding usually occurs between ____.
e: Covalent bonding usually occurs between non-metals. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: If two hydrogen atoms are approaching one another, ____ forces act on the atoms at the same time.
e: If two hydrogen atoms are approaching one another, three forces act on the atoms at the same time. Three is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: When the hydrogen atoms are too close to each other, the ____ interaction between two nuclei becomes so strong that it pushes them apart.
e: When the hydrogen atoms are too close to each other, the repulsive interaction between two nuclei becomes so strong that it pushes them apart. Repulsive is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: Consequently, there is an optimum distance between two nuclei called the ____ where net attractive forces are maximised and the most stable covalent bond is formed in the H-H molecule.
e: Consequently, there is an optimum distance between two nuclei called the bond length where net attractive forces are maximised and the most stable covalent bond is formed in the H-H molecule. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: In covalent bonding, the outermost orbitals of the atoms ____ so that unpaired valence electrons in each of the bonding atoms can be shared, whereas the paired valence electrons are not involved in bonding.
e: In covalent bonding, the outermost orbitals of the atoms overlap so that unpaired valence electrons in each of the bonding atoms can be shared, whereas the paired valence electrons are not involved in bonding. Valence electrons sit in the outermost shell, and those are the electrons that actually form bonds.

q: By overlapping orbitals, the outer shells of all the bonding atoms are filled with valence electrons by following the ____ rule.
e: By overlapping orbitals, the outer shells of all the bonding atoms are filled with valence electrons by following the octet rule. Valence electrons sit in the outermost shell, and those are the electrons that actually form bonds.

q: The covalent bonds can be single bonds or ____ covalent bonds, namely double bonds and triple bonds.
e: The covalent bonds can be single bonds or multiple covalent bonds, namely double bonds and triple bonds. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: In single covalent bonds, only ____ pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.
e: In single covalent bonds, only one pair of electrons is shared between two atoms. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: The length of the bond is determined by the number of ____ electrons.
e: The length of the bond is determined by the number of bonded electrons. Bonded is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: The higher the number of bonded electrons, the stronger the attraction between the two atoms and the ____ the bond length.
e: The higher the number of bonded electrons, the stronger the attraction between the two atoms and the shorter the bond length. Shorter is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: In contrast, the bond strength of the triple bond is the ____, followed by the double bond and single bond.
e: In contrast, the bond strength of the triple bond is the highest, followed by the double bond and single bond. Highest is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: A ____ bond, or dative bond, is a special type of covalent bond.
e: A coordinate bond, or dative bond, is a special type of covalent bond. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: A coordinate bond is formed when one of the participating atoms possesses an unshared pair (a ____ pair) of electrons.
e: A coordinate bond is formed when one of the participating atoms possesses an unshared pair (a lone pair) of electrons. In a coordinate, or dative, bond one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair.

q: A coordinate bond is expressed as an ____, $ightarrow$ which indicates the direction in which the electrons are donated.
e: A coordinate bond is expressed as an arrow, ightarrow which indicates the direction in which the electrons are donated. In a coordinate, or dative, bond one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair.

q: The ammonia molecule possesses a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom; it can be donated to a hydrogen ion to produce the ____ ion $NH_4^+$, forming a coordinate bond.
e: The ammonia molecule possesses a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom; it can be donated to a hydrogen ion to produce the ammonium ion NH4+, forming a coordinate bond. In a coordinate, or dative, bond one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair.

q: Similarly, a water ($H_2O$) molecule that possesses two lone pair electrons on the oxygen atom can react with a hydrogen ion, $H^+$, through a coordinate bond, giving a ____ ion, $H_3O^+$.
e: Similarly, a water (H2O) molecule that possesses two lone pair electrons on the oxygen atom can react with a hydrogen ion, H+, through a coordinate bond, giving a hydronium ion, H3O+. In a coordinate, or dative, bond one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair.

q: In addition, molecules with incomplete octets, called ____ molecules, can accept an electron pair from a molecule bearing a lone pair.
e: In addition, molecules with incomplete octets, called electron-deficient molecules, can accept an electron pair from a molecule bearing a lone pair. An electron-deficient molecule does not have enough valence electrons for an octet on the central atom, like BF3.

q: In carbon monoxide, the CO molecule has a triple bond that consists of two covalent bonds and one ____ bond where both electrons come from the O atom.
e: In carbon monoxide, the CO molecule has a triple bond that consists of two covalent bonds and one coordinate bond where both electrons come from the O atom. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: Lewis structures are only ____-dimensional representations of how the valence shell electrons are arranged around individual atoms in a molecule or an ion.
e: Lewis structures are only two-dimensional representations of how the valence shell electrons are arranged around individual atoms in a molecule or an ion. Valence describes the outer-shell electrons that actually form bonds.

q: In a Lewis structure, a covalent bond is described by writing each shared electron pair either as a pair of two dots between symbols of two atoms or as a ____ connecting them.
e: In a Lewis structure, a covalent bond is described by writing each shared electron pair either as a pair of two dots between symbols of two atoms or as a line connecting them. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: Some molecules that deviate from the octet rule, such as electron-deficient molecules and ____ valence shell molecules can occur.
e: Some molecules that deviate from the octet rule, such as electron-deficient molecules and expanded valence shell molecules can occur. An electron-deficient molecule does not have enough valence electrons for an octet on the central atom, like BF3.

q: The central atom in an electron-deficient molecule has valence electrons of ____ than 8, and that in an expanded valence shell molecule has valence electrons of more than 8.
e: The central atom in an electron-deficient molecule has valence electrons of less than 8, and that in an expanded valence shell molecule has valence electrons of more than 8. An electron-deficient molecule does not have enough valence electrons for an octet on the central atom, like BF3.

q: The molecular shape in which the atoms and electron pairs exist in a ____-dimensional arrangement can be predicted by using the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory.
e: The molecular shape in which the atoms and electron pairs exist in a three-dimensional arrangement can be predicted by using the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory. VSEPR says electron pairs around a central atom push apart, and that repulsion sets the molecular shape.

q: It is based on the idea that the three-dimensional geometry of a molecule is mostly determined by the ____ interactions of the electron pairs around a central atom.
e: It is based on the idea that the three-dimensional geometry of a molecule is mostly determined by the repulsive interactions of the electron pairs around a central atom. Repulsive is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: The repulsive interaction of electron pairs increases in the order of bonding pair-bonding pair < lone pair-bonding pair < ____.
e: The repulsive interaction of electron pairs increases in the order of bonding pair-bonding pair < lone pair-bonding pair < lone pair-lone pair. A bonding pair is the electron pair shared between two atoms in a covalent bond.

q: The lone pairs are ____ on the central atom while each bonding pair is shared between two atoms.
e: The lone pairs are localised on the central atom while each bonding pair is shared between two atoms. A bonding pair is the electron pair shared between two atoms in a covalent bond.

q: These lone pairs of electrons in a molecule occupy ____ space compared with the bonding pairs of electrons.
e: These lone pairs of electrons in a molecule occupy more space compared with the bonding pairs of electrons. A bonding pair is the electron pair shared between two atoms in a covalent bond.

q: All diatomic molecules represent two points in space and are joined by a straight line, i.e., they are ____.
e: All diatomic molecules represent two points in space and are joined by a straight line,, they are linear. Linear is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: In this type, it has only two bonding pairs without ____ pairs.
e: In this type, it has only two bonding pairs without lone pairs. A bonding pair is the electron pair shared between two atoms in a covalent bond.

q: Thus, the shape of $BeCl_2$ is ____.
e: Thus, the shape of BeCl2 is linear. Linear is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: In the $CO_2$ molecule, there are ____ bonding pairs (two double bonds) without lone pairs.
e: In the CO2 molecule, there are four bonding pairs (two double bonds) without lone pairs. A bonding pair is the electron pair shared between two atoms in a covalent bond.

q: If the lone pair is present in these types, the molecular shapes are not the ____ as the geometry of electron pairs.
e: If the lone pair is present in these types, the molecular shapes are not the same as the geometry of electron pairs. Equal forward and reverse rates keep concentrations the same at equilibrium.

q: For example, $AX_3$ has a triangular planar and $AX_2E$, where E represents a lone pair, has a ____ (bent).
e: For example, AX3 has a triangular planar and AX2E, where E represents a lone pair, has a V-shape (bent). A lone pair sits on an atom and is not shared in a bond, but it still takes space and can bend the shape.

q: Some elements occur in solids where the atoms are held together by single covalent bonds, existing as ____ structures.
e: Some elements occur in solids where the atoms are held together by single covalent bonds, existing as giant structures. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: For example, in a diamond, each carbon atom is joined to ____ other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds, and the carbon atoms form a regular tetrahedral network resulting in a giant structure.
e: For example, in a diamond, each carbon atom is joined to four other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds, and the carbon atoms form a regular tetrahedral network resulting in a giant structure. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: In the case of graphite, it has a layer and planar structure formed by joining each carbon atom to the other ____ carbon atoms by covalent bonds.
e: In the case of graphite, it has a layer and planar structure formed by joining each carbon atom to the other three carbon atoms by covalent bonds. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: Each layer is formed with ____ rings of carbon atoms.
e: Each layer is formed with hexagonal rings of carbon atoms. Hexagonal is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: There are weak ____ forces between the layers, which give rise to a giant structure.
e: There are weak van der Waals forces between the layers, which give rise to a giant structure. Van der Waals forces are weak intermolecular attractions, including dipole-dipole, ion-dipole, and London forces.

q: In contrast to diamond, graphite has ____-moving electrons in each layer.
e: In contrast to diamond, graphite has free-moving electrons in each layer. Free is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: That is why graphite can ____ electricity.
e: That is why graphite can conduct electricity. Conduct is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: Silicon(IV) oxide, $SiO_2$ (silica or quartz) is an example of a ____ covalent molecule.
e: Silicon(IV) oxide, SiO2 (silica or quartz) is an example of a giant covalent molecule. Covalent bonding is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: In quartz, each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, but each oxygen atom is bonded to only ____ silicon atoms.
e: In quartz, each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, but each oxygen atom is bonded to only two silicon atoms. Two is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: The oxygen atoms are formed as ____ between the tetrahedrally bonded silicon atoms.
e: The oxygen atoms are formed as bridges between the tetrahedrally bonded silicon atoms. Bridges is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: Molecules in a substance are formed by joining atoms together, and there are attractive and ____ forces that arise between the molecules.
e: Molecules in a substance are formed by joining atoms together, and there are attractive and repulsive forces that arise between the molecules. Repulsive is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: A covalent bond within a molecule is described as a pair of electrons ____ between the atoms.
e: A covalent bond within a molecule is described as a pair of electrons shared between the atoms. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: If the atoms are not identical, the electrons will not be ____ shared.
e: If the atoms are not identical, the electrons will not be equally shared. Equally is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: The atom with the greater share of the electrons will be slightly ____ and the other atom will be slightly positive.
e: The atom with the greater share of the electrons will be slightly negative and the other atom will be slightly positive. A negative sign marks heat leaving the system, or a falling concentration, depending on the equation.

q: Thus, bond polarity within a molecule results in a ____ of charge over the molecule.
e: Thus, bond polarity within a molecule results in a separation of charge over the molecule. Separation is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: Depending on the difference in ____ between two bonded atoms, covalent bonds can be polar or non-polar.
e: Depending on the difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms, covalent bonds can be polar or non-polar. Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls shared bonding electrons toward itself.

q: If two different non-metal atoms are bonded, then the atom with the ____ electronegativity will attract the shared electron pair more strongly.
e: If two different non-metal atoms are bonded, then the atom with the higher electronegativity will attract the shared electron pair more strongly. Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls shared bonding electrons toward itself.

q: The bond becomes more polar as the difference in electronegativity values of the atoms in a covalent bond ____.
e: The bond becomes more polar as the difference in electronegativity values of the atoms in a covalent bond increases. More successful collisions per second make the rate rise.

q: In a covalent bond formed between two similar non-metal atoms, the shared electron pair is ____ attracted to the two atoms resulting in a non-polar covalent bond.
e: In a covalent bond formed between two similar non-metal atoms, the shared electron pair is equally attracted to the two atoms resulting in a non-polar covalent bond. In a non-polar covalent bond the two atoms share the electron pair evenly.

q: As a result of the dipole formed in a polar covalent bond, the bond possesses the ____.
e: As a result of the dipole formed in a polar covalent bond, the bond possesses the dipole moment. In a polar covalent bond the shared electrons sit closer to the more electronegative atom.

q: The direction of arrow points to the ____ end of the dipole.
e: The direction of arrow points to the negative end of the dipole. A negative sign marks heat leaving the system, or a falling concentration, depending on the equation.

q: However, any non-polar covalent bond has a ____ dipole moment.
e: However, any non-polar covalent bond has a zero dipole moment. In a non-polar covalent bond the two atoms share the electron pair evenly.

q: All diatomic molecules containing polar covalent bonds are ____ molecules since they have dipole moments.
e: All diatomic molecules containing polar covalent bonds are polar molecules since they have dipole moments. In a polar covalent bond the shared electrons sit closer to the more electronegative atom.

q: In the case of polyatomic molecules, their dipole moments depend not only on the individual bond dipoles but also on the ____ of the molecules.
e: In the case of polyatomic molecules, their dipole moments depend not only on the individual bond dipoles but also on the shape of the molecules. Dipole moment measures how polar a bond or molecule is.

q: In such cases, the dipole moment of a molecule is the ____ sum of the dipole moments of various bonds.
e: In such cases, the dipole moment of a molecule is the vector sum of the dipole moments of various bonds. Dipole moment measures how polar a bond or molecule is.

q: For example, the $H_2O$ molecule has a ____ shape.
e: For example, the H2O molecule has a bent shape. Bent is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: In the case of the $CO_2$ molecule, it is ____ and the two polar bonds are arranged symmetrically.
e: In the case of the CO2 molecule, it is linear and the two polar bonds are arranged symmetrically. Linear is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: The two equal bond dipoles point in ____ directions and cancel the effect of each other.
e: The two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel the effect of each other. Two electrons in one orbital must spin opposite ways.

q: Thus, the dipole moment of $CO_2$ is ____, and it is a non-polar molecule.
e: Thus, the dipole moment of CO2 is zero, and it is a non-polar molecule. Dipole moment measures how polar a bond or molecule is.

q: Intermolecular forces are forces that act between a molecule and another ____.
e: Intermolecular forces are forces that act between a molecule and another molecule. Intermolecular forces tug neighbouring molecules or ions together; they are not the bonds inside a molecule.

q: Van der Waals forces are weak forces which include dipole-dipole interaction, ion-dipole interaction, and ____ dispersion forces.
e: Van der Waals forces are weak forces which include dipole-dipole interaction, ion-dipole interaction, and London dispersion forces. Van der Waals forces are weak intermolecular attractions, including dipole-dipole, ion-dipole, and London forces.

q: Dipole-dipole interactions are formed when two ____ molecules interact with each other in space.
e: Dipole-dipole interactions are formed when two dipolar molecules interact with each other in space. Dipole-dipole attraction lines up the positive end of one polar molecule with the negative end of another.

q: When this occurs, the partially negative portion of one of the polar molecules is attracted to the partially ____ portion of the second polar molecule.
e: When this occurs, the partially negative portion of one of the polar molecules is attracted to the partially positive portion of the second polar molecule. A positive enthalpy change means the system absorbed heat.

q: This type of intermolecular force is formed from the interaction between an ____ and a dipole molecule.
e: This type of intermolecular force is formed from the interaction between an ion and a dipole molecule. Intermolecular forces tug neighbouring molecules or ions together; they are not the bonds inside a molecule.

q: The weakest intermolecular forces that can be formed between atoms, as well as non-polar molecules, are known as ____ dispersion forces.
e: The weakest intermolecular forces that can be formed between atoms, as well as non-polar molecules, are known as London dispersion forces. Intermolecular forces tug neighbouring molecules or ions together; they are not the bonds inside a molecule.

q: Because of the constant motion of the electrons, an atom can develop ____ (instantaneous) dipole when the electrons are distributed unsymmetrically about the nucleus.
e: Because of the constant motion of the electrons, an atom can develop temporary (instantaneous) dipole when the electrons are distributed unsymmetrically about the nucleus. A dipole is a plus end and a minus end separated in space.

q: Then, this instantaneous dipole of the first atom can ____ a second atom to be distorted because electrons repel one another.
e: Then, this instantaneous dipole of the first atom can induce a second atom to be distorted because electrons repel one another. A dipole is a plus end and a minus end separated in space.

q: This electrostatic attraction is known as the London dispersion force, also called ____ dipole-induced dipole interaction.
e: This electrostatic attraction is known as the London dispersion force, also called induced dipole-induced dipole interaction. London dispersion forces are weak temporary-dipole attractions found in every substance.

q: These London dispersion forces can occur between ____ molecules such as halogens, carbon dioxide, nitrogen, methane, and noble gases.
e: These London dispersion forces can occur between non-polar molecules such as halogens, carbon dioxide, nitrogen, methane, and noble gases. London dispersion forces are weak temporary-dipole attractions found in every substance.

q: Due to these weak attractive forces, non-polar substances can ____ into liquids and can freeze into solids when the temperature is lowered sufficiently.
e: Due to these weak attractive forces, non-polar substances can condense into liquids and can freeze into solids when the temperature is lowered sufficiently. Higher temperature means a larger fraction of particles have energy at least Ea.

q: Hence, London dispersion forces are ____ dipole-dipole interactions that exist between all atoms and molecules.
e: Hence, London dispersion forces are instantaneous dipole-dipole interactions that exist between all atoms and molecules. London dispersion forces are weak temporary-dipole attractions found in every substance.

q: The formation of hydrogen bonds between covalent molecules requires: (1) the first molecule has hydrogen attached to a high ____ atom (F, O, or N).
e: The formation of hydrogen bonds between covalent molecules requires: (1) the first molecule has hydrogen attached to a high electronegative atom (F, O, or N). A hydrogen bond is the strong intermolecular pull from H attached to N, O, or F toward another N, O, or F.

q: ...and (2) the second molecule possesses a ____ pair of electrons on a small electronegative atom (F, O, or N).
e: ...and (2) the second molecule possesses a lone pair of electrons on a small electronegative atom (F, O, or N). Lone is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: Because of the highly electronegativity difference between H atom and bonded F, O, or N atom, the bond is very highly ____.
e: Because of the highly electronegativity difference between H atom and bonded F, O, or N atom, the bond is very highly polarised. Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls shared bonding electrons toward itself.

q: Hydrogen bonding can occur as both intermolecular and ____ forces.
e: Hydrogen bonding can occur as both intermolecular and intramolecular forces. Intermolecular forces tug neighbouring molecules or ions together; they are not the bonds inside a molecule.

q: A hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole-dipole interaction that occurs between polar molecules and is ____ than van der Waals forces.
e: A hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole-dipole interaction that occurs between polar molecules and is stronger than van der Waals forces. Van der Waals forces are weak intermolecular attractions, including dipole-dipole, ion-dipole, and London forces.

q: The hydrogen bond is weaker than a covalent bond and is the ____ of all intermolecular forces.
e: The hydrogen bond is weaker than a covalent bond and is the strongest of all intermolecular forces. Intermolecular forces tug neighbouring molecules or ions together; they are not the bonds inside a molecule.

q: Most of the metals are ____ at room temperature, and therefore, there must be some sort of bonding between these metal atoms.
e: Most of the metals are solids at room temperature, and therefore, there must be some sort of bonding between these metal atoms. Higher temperature means a larger fraction of particles have energy at least Ea.

q: These metal atoms are held together in solid ____ form by a metallic bonding.
e: These metal atoms are held together in solid crystalline form by a metallic bonding. Metallic bonding is the attraction between metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons.

q: In a metallic bond, the atoms do not share or ____ electrons to bond together.
e: In a metallic bond, the atoms do not share or transfer electrons to bond together. Metallic bonding is the attraction between metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons.

q: The structure of a metallic bond is quite ____ from that of covalent or ionic bonds.
e: The structure of a metallic bond is quite different from that of covalent or ionic bonds. Metallic bonding is the attraction between metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons.

q: In ____ solids, e.g., sodium, magnesium, and aluminium, atoms of metals are present.
e: In metallic solids,, sodium, magnesium, and aluminium, atoms of metals are present. Metallic bonding is metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons.

q: In a metallic bond, the valence electrons of the atoms are very ____ held, forming a common electron cloud.
e: In a metallic bond, the valence electrons of the atoms are very loosely held, forming a common electron cloud. Loosely: valence electrons sit in the outermost shell, and those are the electrons that actually form bonds.

q: These valence electrons move ____ within this electron cloud.
e: These valence electrons move freely within this electron cloud. Valence electrons sit in the outermost shell, and those are the electrons that actually form bonds.

q: These mobile electrons are often described as "a ____ of electrons" which make the metals easily conduct electricity.
e: These mobile electrons are often described as "a sea of electrons" which make the metals easily conduct electricity. Sea is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: The ____ charged metallic nuclei are surrounded by free-moving electrons.
e: The positively charged metallic nuclei are surrounded by free-moving electrons. Positively: metallic bonding is metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons.

q: The bonding results from the ____ of these electrons with the various nuclei.
e: The bonding results from the interaction of these electrons with the various nuclei. Interaction is the chemical word that makes this relationship true.

q: Metals consist of giant structures of atoms that are packed closely together in a regular arrangement called a ____.
e: Metals consist of giant structures of atoms that are packed closely together in a regular arrangement called a lattice. A crystal lattice is the repeating 3D pattern of particles in a solid.

q: The strength of metallic bonding increases with (1) the increasing ____ charge on the ions in the metal lattice.
e: The strength of metallic bonding increases with (1) the increasing positive charge on the ions in the metal lattice. A positive enthalpy change means the system absorbed heat.

q: ...(2) the ____ size of metal ions in the lattice.
e: ...(2) the decreasing size of metal ions in the lattice. A crystal lattice is the repeating 3D pattern of particles in a solid.

q: ...and (3) the increasing number of ____ electrons (valence electrons) per atom.
e: ...and (3) the increasing number of mobile electrons (valence electrons) per atom. Valence electrons sit in the outermost shell, and those are the electrons that actually form bonds.

q: However, the strength of metallic bond is ____ than that of an ionic bond.
e: However, the strength of metallic bond is lower than that of an ionic bond. Aufbau fills lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy ones.

q: Consequently, the melting points of some metals become ____ compared with the ionic compounds.
e: Consequently, the melting points of some metals become lower compared with the ionic compounds. Aufbau fills lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy ones.
